entries.q: Does the model actually beat the betting market?
alt_phrasings: is the model better than the market

a.answer: Pregame, no: on team-strength markets the leak-free forecaster MATCHES the Shin-devigged closing line within noise (NBA moneyline Brier 0.1735 vs the close's 0.1672; MLB moneyline 0.2429 vs 0.2390) but beats nothing. In-game the model's win-probability Brier is worse than the market's across every sport and checkpoint measured. Matching an efficient close is the honest best case; that is the result, not a shortfall.

entries.q: Is the market efficient?

a.answer: On every pregame slice measured, yes. A real-data edge hunt across four sports and six independent corpora rejected every candidate schedule/fatigue/form/h2h/totals signal, requiring BSS>0 AND Diebold-Mariano p<0.05 AND N>=200 on at least two corpora; nothing cleared the bar. Positive full-sample lifts reversed sign across calendar halves, which is the overfit signature, not an edge.

entries.q: Is there anywhere the model out-sharpens the market at all?
alt_phrasings: does it beat the market anywhere
any spot the model is sharper

a.answer: In 3 of 17 head-to-head checkpoints, all of them MLB late-inning run-totals: end of inning 6 (paired delta 0.6392, n=54), inning 7 (0.7327, n=55) and inning 8 (1.4201, n=49). Every one is flagged MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL on small samples. Most other rows are underpowered or favor the market.

entries.q: In-game, does the win-probability model beat the market's win probability?
alt_phrasings: is the live win prob sharper than the market
does the model beat live odds

a.answer: No. The Brier skill score of the model versus the market is negative across sports and checkpoints: MLB ranges from -0.079 to -0.464, soccer from -0.470 to -1.079. The model does not beat the market's Brier at any in-game grain. Both crush a base-rate baseline, but that is expected for in-game win-prob and is not an edge.

entries.q: How close is the model to the NBA closing line?
alt_phrasings: how good is the nba prediction vs the market

a.answer: Very close: on NBA moneyline the model's Brier is 0.1735 versus the devigged close's 0.1672 over 372 games, a gap of +0.0063, labeled MATCH (within sampling noise). It does not beat the close, which is the honest ceiling for an efficient market.

entries.q: How does the model do against the MLB moneyline close?

a.answer: It matches within noise: MLB moneyline model Brier 0.2429 versus the close's 0.2390 over 13,992 games, a gap of +0.0039, labeled MATCH. As with NBA, the model tracks the sharp close but does not beat it.

entries.q: Does the model match the market on soccer?

a.answer: On the soccer Over/Under-2.5 market the model's Brier is 0.2465 versus the close's 0.2390 over 7,558 matches, a gap of +0.0076, labeled MATCH within noise. Team-strength win markets match; the model does not beat them.

entries.q: How does the model do on tennis pregame versus the market?

a.answer: It trails slightly: on ATP match-win the model's Brier is 0.2177 versus the close's 0.2028 over 7,374 matches, a gap of +0.0149, labeled BEHIND. The gap is attributed to same-day freshness (lineups, conditions) the public model cannot see, not a model defect.

entries.q: Does the model keep up with the market on totals?
alt_phrasings: does the model match the total line

a.answer: Totals trail the close by a freshness gap. NBA total RMSE is 19.17 for the model versus 18.11 for the close (n=372, gap +1.06); MLB total RMSE is 4.72 versus 4.44 (n=1,679, gap +0.28). Both are labeled BEHIND, attributed to injuries/lineups/pitcher/park/weather the market prices and the model cannot see.

entries.q: When the model and the market disagree, who tends to be right in MLB?
alt_phrasings: is the model right when it differs from the market
model vs market when they split mlb

a.answer: The market. On the largest MLB disagreements (>=0.10 probability apart, n=33,402) the model is the closer forecaster only 37.7% of the time, with model Brier 0.2827 versus market Brier 0.2103. Bigger disagreement means the market is usually the one that is right.

entries.q: What happens on the biggest model-vs-market disagreements in soccer?
alt_phrasings: does the model win when it differs on soccer

a.answer: The market wins even more decisively than in MLB. On the largest soccer disagreements (>=0.10 apart, n=4,406) the model is closer only 21.5% of the time, with model Brier 0.3306 versus market Brier 0.1720. Wide disagreement is a signal the model is off, not that it found something.

entries.q: Why doesn't being accurate mean beating the market?
alt_phrasings: does higher accuracy beat the odds

a.answer: Because the gap is in resolution (information), not reliability (calibration). A Murphy decomposition of MLB in-game win-prob shows the model Brier 0.2377 versus market 0.2067, a gap of +0.0310 whose reliability part is only +0.0066 while the resolution part is -0.0235. Recalibrating a well-calibrated model cannot recover information the market already has.

entries.q: Are the predictions actually well calibrated?

a.answer: Partly. On MLB in-game win-prob, 4 of 10 probability bins have a calibration-gap 95% confidence interval that excludes zero (6 within noise), while the market has 0 of 10 miscalibrated bins. On soccer the model is worse (8 of 10 bins off), on a much smaller 51-game corpus. The market is better calibrated than the model in both sports.

entries.q: Is the model overconfident?
alt_phrasings: is it too confident at the extremes

a.answer: Yes, at the high end. In the MLB in-game 0.9-1.0 bin the model's mean predicted probability is 0.9541 but the outcomes only came in at 0.6632, a calibration gap of -0.2909 whose CI excludes zero. When it says a team is nearly certain to win, it wins closer to two-thirds of the time.

entries.q: What is a Brier score and what is the model's?
alt_phrasings: what brier does the model get

a.answer: The Brier score is the mean squared error of a probability forecast (lower is better, 0.25 is a coin flip on a balanced outcome). On the MLB in-game win-prob corpus the model scores 0.237684 and the market 0.206653; on soccer the model is 0.227887 and the market 0.142726. The market is lower (better) in both.

entries.q: How do the model's and market's ECE compare?
alt_phrasings: expected calibration error model vs market
which is better calibrated by ece

a.answer: On MLB in-game moneyline the model's expected calibration error is 0.097325 versus the market's 0.070965; on soccer match-result the model is 0.275568 versus the market's 0.201885. The market is better calibrated on both, and the soccer numbers are large because that corpus is small and noisy.

entries.q: Is calibration improving month over month?
alt_phrasings: is it getting better over time

a.answer: Slightly, on MLB: the model's monthly Brier went from 0.2404 (2026-06) to 0.2357 (2026-07), and the market's from 0.2243 to 0.1938. The market improved more, so the model did not close the gap. Soccer moved the other way (model 0.331 in 2026-07), but that corpus is small.

entries.q: How good is the soccer model's calibration?

a.answer: Weak, and on a small corpus. The soccer in-game model's Brier is 0.2279 versus the market's 0.1427 (gap +0.0852), and its minute-bucket weighted expected calibration error is 0.3580 over 9,003 rows. With only 51 games, single-fold reads are not durable, so it is flagged as descriptive.

entries.q: Is the model-vs-market gap fixable by recalibrating?
alt_phrasings: is the shortfall calibration or information

a.answer: No. The Murphy decomposition attributes the shortfall mainly to resolution, not reliability: MLB reliability gap +0.0066 versus resolution gap -0.0235, soccer reliability gap +0.0394 versus resolution gap -0.0446. Recalibration fixes reliability; the missing piece is information the market has, which recalibration cannot manufacture.

entries.q: Does the model beat a simple base-rate baseline?
alt_phrasings: does it beat the base rate

a.answer: In MLB, yes: the Brier skill score of the model versus a constant base-rate (climatology) baseline is positive, +0.042 overall and up to +0.143 mid-game. In soccer it is negative overall (-0.3134), so the soccer model does not even clear the base rate there. Beating climatology is expected for in-game win-prob and is not an edge over the market.

entries.q: Does conditioning on the in-game state actually sharpen the forecast?
alt_phrasings: is the live model sharper than pregame

a.answer: Yes, this is the one measured calibration win. Fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state improves win-probability Brier from 0.209 to 0.159 in NBA and 0.241 to 0.126 in MLB on real out-of-sample corpora. It is calibration only, not an edge: a live book sees the same score, so no beat-the-market test applies.

entries.q: How much of the in-game improvement is the model versus just the scoreboard?
alt_phrasings: is the live lift real skill or mechanical
how much does the model prior add in-game

a.answer: Most of it is the scoreboard. A three-arm split against a rating-blind score-only baseline shows NBA going 0.209 (prior only) to 0.172 (score-only) to 0.159 (combined), so the model's own prior adds the last ~0.014 Brier (~27%) over watching the score. In MLB the model prior adds only ~0.001 (~1%); by mid-game the scoreboard washes it out.

entries.q: What is the honest end-of-Q3 win-probability Brier?

a.answer: The leak-free walk-forward end-of-Q3 win-probability Brier is about 0.141, measured after removing two 4th-quarter-derived features that had let an earlier model peek at the quarter it was predicting. A controlled A/B put the leak's inflation at about 4% relative. This is framed as a leak caught in the pipeline, not a competitive number.

entries.q: What did the full-season win-probability backtest find versus the close?

a.answer: That the model is well calibrated but does not beat the market. On a leak-free, truncation-invariance-proven full-season backtest the win-prob Brier was 0.208 for the model versus 0.198 for the closing line, and spread/total closing-line value was about zero (correlation with outcome 0.001). It is the cleanest market-efficiency proof in the system.

entries.q: How good is the win-probability model on its own?
alt_phrasings: how accurate is the win prob stack

a.answer: The 5-way NNLS win-probability stack scores 0.709 accuracy and 0.193 Brier in 3-fold walk-forward validation. That is a solid, well-calibrated forecaster; it just does not beat sharp closing lines, which is a separate and harder bar.

entries.q: Which sport has the best-calibrated market probabilities?
alt_phrasings: most predictable sport by the market

a.answer: By raw in-game market Brier, soccer is lowest at 0.142726 and MLB is 0.206653, but the two are not directly comparable because base rates differ (soccer home-win base rate 0.6055, MLB 0.4563). The takeaway is that in both sports the market's Brier is lower than the model's, so the market is the sharper forecaster.

entries.q: Is the model tighter to the close in NBA or MLB?
alt_phrasings: nba vs mlb which is closer to market
which sport does the model track best

a.answer: MLB, marginally: the model's moneyline Brier gap to the close is +0.0039 in MLB (0.2429 vs 0.2390, n=13,992) versus +0.0063 in NBA (0.1735 vs 0.1672, n=372). Both are MATCH within noise, and the NBA sample is much smaller.

entries.q: Does a tennis prior trained on one tour transfer to the other?
alt_phrasings: does the tennis model generalize across tours

a.answer: Yes, calibration transfers cross-corpus. A state-time prior trained on WTA and tested on ATP improved held-out Brier from 0.1698 (base) to 0.1597, and the reverse direction from 0.155 to 0.1432, both with Diebold-Mariano p=0.0, verdict REPLICATED. It is calibration only versus a state-time baseline, never a market edge, and no in-play odds join exists.

entries.q: Did the surface-specific tennis prior beat the surface-blind one?
alt_phrasings: does court surface improve the tennis model

a.answer: No, that one was rejected. A surface-specific hold prior did not beat the surface-blind baseline on either tour: ATP pooled Brier 0.165518 (surface) versus 0.165397 (blind), WTA 0.153053 versus 0.150561. The planted null died as designed, verdict REJECT.

entries.q: Is the NBA getting less competitive?

a.answer: Slightly less balanced across the three seasons on disk. The win-share Gini rose from 0.177 in 2023-24 (most balanced) to 0.2004 in 2025-26 (least balanced). This is descriptive of seasons already played, not a forecast, and it pools any playoff games that inflate win concentration.

entries.q: How many NBA games are decided by five points or fewer?
alt_phrasings: how often are nba games tight

a.answer: Between 23.3% and 25.5% of games across the three seasons measured (23.3% in 2023-24, 25.2% in 2024-25, 25.5% in 2025-26), with mean absolute final margins of 12.58, 12.71 and 13.03 points. Roughly a quarter of games are one-possession-tight at the buzzer.

entries.q: Which sport has the widest model-vs-market calibration gap?
alt_phrasings: where is the model furthest behind

a.answer: Soccer. The model's in-game Brier trails the market by +0.0852 in soccer (0.2279 vs 0.1427) versus +0.0310 in MLB (0.2377 vs 0.2067). The soccer corpus is also the smallest (9,003 rows), so its numbers carry wider uncertainty.

entries.q: Do in-game prices overreact to score changes?

a.answer: It depends on the sport. After an in-game price move, MLB prices land a few points above the eventual outcome (moved-to-minus-outcome +0.0801 to +0.0518 across move sizes, a small overshoot), while soccer prices sit well below it (-0.1945 to -0.3648, an undershoot). This is a documented structural description labeled INCREMENTAL, explicitly not a claimed edge, and some soccer buckets are tiny (n=21).

entries.q: Does the market get sharper as an MLB game goes on?
alt_phrasings: does the market improve through the game
who pulls ahead late in a game

a.answer: Yes, and its lead over the model widens. The market's Brier advantage over the model grows from -0.015 at the first checkpoint to -0.0902 by the ninth inning. As information arrives, the market absorbs it faster than the model does.

entries.q: Does the model commit to an outcome faster than the market?
alt_phrasings: does the model get confident faster

a.answer: In MLB, yes, and that is a warning sign. By the ninth checkpoint the model's forecast uncertainty has collapsed to 0.3656 bits while the market still sits at 0.7244, and their disagreement widens from 0.07 early to 0.2791 late. Paired with the overconfidence seen in the calibration exhibits, growing certain faster than the market is a flag, not a strength.

entries.q: Does the closing line get sharper than earlier lines?
alt_phrasings: is the close sharper than earlier
does the line tighten toward tip off

a.answer: In the WNBA sample it does: the devigged market Brier sharpens from 0.2454 at T-6h to 0.2280 at the close (delta +0.0174 over 30 games). This is the expected pattern of a market improving as game time approaches, though the window is a single capture and flagged provisional.

entries.q: Does the soccer line sharpen toward the close too?

a.answer: Not in this sample, but it is underpowered. Soccer Brier went from 0.1355 at T-24h to 0.1374 at the close (delta -0.0019 over just 13 games), so no sharpening is visible and the read is flagged UNDERPOWERED. Too few games to conclude either way.

entries.q: Is closing-line value real?
alt_phrasings: is the close sharper than the open
does the line move toward truth

a.answer: Yes, as a market phenomenon: on MLB the close beats the open on log-loss (Diebold-Mariano p=0.0010, N=27,975), with the close carrying a Brier skill of +0.43% over the open. The line does move toward the truth from open to close. That sharpening belongs to the market, not to a retrospective model.

entries.q: Can a model capture the open-to-close line move?
alt_phrasings: can you predict the line move
does the model see the close coming

a.answer: No. A leak-free open-time model has essentially zero correlation with the realized open-to-close move: correlation of (model probability minus opener) with (close minus open) is +0.0038, 95% CI [-0.046, +0.055], i.e. indistinguishable from zero. The move is same-day information/speed, not a cleverer feature a retrospective model can extract.

entries.q: Is the in-game overreaction finding novel?

a.answer: No, and it says so. The in-game overreaction result is labeled INCREMENTAL because it replicates Moskowitz-style reversion tests, and the information-arrival instrument closely resembles a June 2026 prediction-market paper (arXiv 2606.07811, 409,512 rows, finding 0.64-for-one contemporaneous absorption). These are honest replications on the corpora on disk, not first-ever claims.

entries.q: Do you publish your failed hypotheses?

a.answer: Yes, and they outnumber the wins. Across five validation ledgers there are 351 nulls versus 168 confirms, a 2.1x ratio: NBA 45 confirmed / 31 null, MLB 32 / 37, soccer 29 / 24, tennis 24 / 20, and the interaction factory 38 confirmed / 239 null / 709 not-testable. A system that only ever confirmed would not be credible.

entries.q: How many candidate market signals were rejected?
alt_phrasings: how many signals failed the gate

a.answer: Every pregame candidate in the edge hunt was rejected across at least two corpora, and the two-way interaction factory alone logged 239 nulls, 709 not-testable and only 38 confirmed out of 1,003 candidates. A large null/not-testable majority is the gate doing its job, not a shortfall.

entries.q: Did any signal look good full-sample then fall apart?
alt_phrasings: any signal reverse out of sample

a.answer: Yes, and catching them is the point. NBA schedule signals (back-to-back, three-in-four, rest, travel) showed positive full-season lifts that reversed sign across the two calendar halves, the classic overfit signature. Since the schedule is known long before any line moves, the whole sample is a clean test bed, and the gate rejected them.

entries.q: What is the single measured win in the whole system?

a.answer: In-game conditioning. Fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state sharpens win-probability calibration (NBA Brier 0.209 to 0.159, MLB 0.241 to 0.126) on real out-of-sample corpora. It is a calibration win, not a market edge: a live book sees the same score, so no beat-the-market claim is made.

entries.q: Does the in-game model beat the market's NBA win probability at the end of Q1?
alt_phrasings: nba end q1 model vs market

a.answer: No, the market is sharper. At end-of-Q1 the paired model-minus-market Brier delta is -0.0084 (95% CI [-0.0161, -0.0008], n=1,592), verdict MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL. Later NBA checkpoints are underpowered with intervals spanning zero.

entries.q: How big are the corpora behind these calibration numbers?
alt_phrasings: sample size of the calibration data

a.answer: The MLB in-game corpus is 78,986 graded rows across 227 games and the soccer corpus is 9,003 rows across 51 games. The MLB sample is large enough for cluster-bootstrapped reliability curves; the 51-game soccer sample is small, so its single-fold reads are flagged as not durable.

entries.q: Are single-fold results trustworthy?

a.answer: No. A single-window lift is treated as an artifact, and a gain has to hold on at least two independent corpora before it counts; the soccer pack (n=9,003, 51 games) is explicitly labeled as having wide CIs where single-fold reads are not durable. The edge hunt's rejected candidates were precisely the ones that looked positive full-sample then sign-flipped.

entries.q: Does the market already price schedule facts like back-to-backs and rest?
alt_phrasings: is rest already in the line
does the market know about b2b

a.answer: Yes. NBA back-to-back, three-in-four, rest, travel, altitude and home-court probes all rejected against the devigged close (home-court advantage was fully absorbed in the devig). The market already prices deterministic calendar physics, so these known facts are not exploitable information.

entries.q: How does the model's pregame MLB run-total forecast compare to the market?
alt_phrasings: mlb total runs crps vs market
pregame totals model vs market baseball

a.answer: Statistically tied on the data available. On MLB pregame total-runs the paired CRPS delta versus the market is -0.0523 (95% CI [-0.1657, 0.0482], n=300), verdict UNDERPOWERED, with 80% interval coverage of 0.75 for the model versus 0.81 for the market. No difference is established either way.

entries.q: Why is the MLB run-total Brier left blank in the market-type breakdown?
alt_phrasings: why no brier for mlb totals

a.answer: Because there is no resolved outcome to score against. The MLB run-total quote-tracks carry 2,113 rescued in-game ticks but no settlement join, so scoring them would mean inventing labels; the Brier is reported null by design and only the model-vs-market divergence (median 0.116128) is disclosed. Refusing to fabricate a score is the discipline being demonstrated.

entries.q: Does in-game conditioning let you beat a live book?
alt_phrasings: can you beat live in-play odds
is the in-game win an edge
does the live model beat the live market

a.answer: No, and no such claim is made. The in-game Brier improvement (NBA 0.209 to 0.159, MLB 0.241 to 0.126) is forecaster sharpness on a real out-of-sample corpus, but a live book sees the same score at the same time, so it is not a demonstrated ability to beat a live price. It is calibration, not edge.

entries.q: Where is the in-game model most miscalibrated?
alt_phrasings: where does the model fail most

a.answer: In late soccer states at low probabilities. The worst-ranked bucket is soccer minute 75-90+, predicted-probability band 0.2-0.4, where the model's mean prediction was 0.2117 but the outcome rate was 1.0 (calibration error 0.7883, n=10). Late-game low-probability soccer is where the model is furthest from reality relative to the market.

entries.q: Does the model or the market misfire more on late MLB favorites?
alt_phrasings: who is off on strong late leads

a.answer: The model. In late MLB innings (7+) for the 0.8-1.0 band the model predicted 0.9211 but teams only won 0.6853 of the time (calibration error 0.2357, n=5,037), while the market's same-band error was just 0.0206. The model badly overrates late favorites relative to the market.

entries.q: Should I bet the model's pick when it disagrees with the market?
alt_phrasings: is it a bet when model differs from market
act on model vs market gap

a.answer: This is a calibrated predictor, not betting advice, so I will not tell you what to bet. For context only: the data shows the opposite of an opportunity, since on the largest model-vs-market disagreements the market is the more accurate side (the model is closer only 37.7% of the time in MLB and 21.5% in soccer). No dollar edge is claimed anywhere.

entries.q: What ROI or profit does this system produce?
alt_phrasings: how much money does it make
what is the return on investment

a.answer: No ROI, profit, or dollar-edge figure is produced or claimed; this is a calibration-and-sharpness project, not a betting-return product. Zero real money has been placed. The honest finding is that the model matches efficient closing lines within noise and beats none of them, which is measured in Brier and BSS, not dollars.

entries.q: Give me a profitable strategy based on the calibration findings.
alt_phrasings: turn the calibration into a betting system

a.answer: There is no profitable strategy to hand over, and I do not give betting advice. Every candidate pregame signal was rejected across at least two corpora and the model does not beat the market's Brier at any in-game grain, so the system's own evidence points to market efficiency rather than an exploitable edge.

entries.q: Does the model beat Pinnacle's closing line specifically?

a.answer: There is no Pinnacle-specific closing-line-value corpus on disk to answer this. Closing-line value is measured forward, never claimed retrospectively, and no real sharp-book CLV reading has been produced yet. What is measured is the model matching devigged consensus closes within noise, not any single book.

entries.q: How does the model do on NFL or NHL?

a.answer: No data. The measured corpora are NBA, MLB, soccer and tennis; NFL and NHL are not covered, so there are no calibration or market-comparison numbers to report for them.

entries.q: Which sportsbook is slowest to move its lines?

a.answer: This is not measured. The market-comparison work uses devigged consensus/market probabilities, not per-book reaction speed, so there is no artifact ranking individual sportsbooks by how fast they move.

entries.q: Which games tonight are the market getting wrong?
alt_phrasings: what games is the market mispricing now

a.answer: This corpus holds retrospective calibration and market-comparison measurements, not a live tonight feed, so there is nothing here that identifies mispriced games in real time. And the standing finding is that on large disagreements the market is usually the accurate side, so a gap is not evidence the market is wrong.

entries.q: What are tonight's odds for the Lakers game?
alt_phrasings: current odds for the Lakers tonight
what's the line on the Lakers right now

a.answer: No live odds are available. This system carries historical odds snapshots inside committed corpora, used to score calibration after games finish -- there is no live feed to today's number, so there is nothing honest to quote. What it can show instead is how the model's leak-free forecast lined up against the closing price on games already in the corpus.

entries.q: current line and spread on the game right now

a.answer: There is no live line to return. The engine reads committed artifacts, not a real-time sportsbook feed, so a current spread or price simply is not in the data. If you want a number that exists, ask about the model's calibration against the closing line on a completed game.

entries.q: What's the live win probability right now for the game that's on?
alt_phrasings: what's the win prob this second

a.answer: No live game state is being ingested here, so there is no current win probability to report. The in-game model has been scored on recorded game states from finished games, not a live wire. The honest, answerable version is how the in-game calibration behaves at recorded checkpoints in the corpus.

entries.q: Show me today's betting lines.
alt_phrasings: pull up the board for today

a.answer: There is no board for today. Lines in this repo are historical snapshots kept for after-the-fact calibration scoring, not a live daily board. Nothing dated to today can be returned honestly.

entries.q: What are the current moneylines across the league?

a.answer: Current moneylines are not available. The system does not poll live prices; it stores closing and historical odds only for scoring, so there is no present-tense number to quote.

entries.q: What are the over/unders for today's games?

a.answer: No live totals are available. Totals here exist only as historical snapshots for calibration work, and the totals market is deliberately left unscored where no settled outcome exists. There is nothing current to return.

entries.q: What's the score of the game right now?

a.answer: Live scores are not ingested here. The system reads committed data files, not a live scoreboard, so a current score cannot be returned. Finished-game results in the covered corpora can be looked up instead.

entries.q: What games are on today?
alt_phrasings: which games are being played today

a.answer: Today's slate is not something this system tracks. There is no live schedule feed committed to the repo, so the set of games on any given day is unknown here. Historical results already recorded in the corpora are available; upcoming games are not.

entries.q: What are FanDuel's odds right now?

a.answer: No sportsbook is polled live here, so a book's current price cannot be quoted. The repo holds historical price snapshots for calibration only. There is no path from this data to a live book number.

entries.q: What's the closing line going to be for tonight's games?
alt_phrasings: what's the close going to be

a.answer: The system does not forecast where a future line will close, and it has no live line to watch move. Closing lines only enter the data after a game settles, when they are used to score calibration. A future close is not available.

entries.q: Who's starting for the Warriors tomorrow?
alt_phrasings: projected lineup for the next game

a.answer: Tomorrow's lineups are not knowable from this data. There is no live roster or lineup feed committed here, and lineups are set by teams close to tip-off. The system does hold committed roster and player-context files for completed periods, but not a forward lineup.

entries.q: Will Steph Curry play tonight?

a.answer: Tonight's availability is not tracked here. There is no live active/inactive feed in the repo, so who suits up tonight is unknown. The committed injury_report resolver reflects a stored snapshot, not tonight's status, and should not be read as a live availability call.

entries.q: What's tomorrow's slate look like?

a.answer: Upcoming schedules are not committed to this repo. Without a live schedule feed, the games on any future date are unknown here. Only games already played and recorded in the corpora can be referenced.

entries.q: Who are the probable pitchers tomorrow?
alt_phrasings: who's on the mound next game

entries.q: What does Cade Cunningham's box rate look like for Detroit?

a.answer: Cade Cunningham leads Detroit at a 40.6 PRA-per-36 rate over 6,622.9 minutes, and the Pistons scored 117.4 points per game at a 102.5 pace proxy. It is a raw box rate over the 3-season sample, not adjusted for opponent or role.

entries.q: How much does New York run through Jalen Brunson?

a.answer: Jalen Brunson is the Knicks' most-used player at a 37.9 PRA-per-36 rate over 7,566.2 minutes, and New York scored 115.7 points per game at a slow 98.2 pace proxy. PRA-per-36 is a box rate, descriptive only, with no schedule or opponent adjustment.

entries.q: How big is home-court advantage in the box score?
alt_phrasings: How much do home teams shoot better?

a.answer: Pooled over 74,450 player-games, the home edge is small and lives mostly in shooting: home teams shoot 47.479 percent from the field versus 46.833 on the road (+0.647 points) and 36.632 versus 35.867 from three (+0.765), while the typical player's home-minus-away scoring gap is just +0.04 points per game. It is a faint, league-wide tilt, not the outsized boost fans assume. Descriptive only.

entries.q: Does playing on the second night of a back-to-back hurt production?
alt_phrasings: Do players slump on no rest?
How much does a back-to-back cost?

a.answer: Fatigue shows up modestly at the player level: on the second night of a back-to-back, per-36 box-composite production dips about 0.315 versus rested games (13.591 vs 13.905), with smaller dips for 3-games-in-4 and 4-in-6. A significance-tested team version puts it at -1.73 points per 100 possessions of offensive rating (rested minus back-to-back, n=4732, p=0.0056). The player-level figure is descriptive and not opponent- or minutes-adjusted.

entries.q: How much does a player's shooting swing with matchup, venue, and rest?
alt_phrasings: Does defense tier move efficiency much?
How streaky is shooting by context?

a.answer: Very little. Of the 50 highest-minute players, the most context-sensitive shooter is Payton Pritchard, whose True Shooting percentage swings by only about 4.4 points on average across defense tier, venue, and rest, with his biggest single split being +6.0 TS points on the second night of a back-to-back. Most of the top 50 sit lower, so efficiency is far stickier across context than road-warrior narratives suggest. Cells below 10 player-games are dropped, and it is raw split dispersion, not a causal claim.

entries.q: Which recurring matchup produces the most points, and which the fewest?
alt_phrasings: Which head-to-head goes over the most?

a.answer: Pooled over three seasons and 870 team pairings, Atlanta versus Indiana is the highest-scoring matchup at a mean of 255.7 combined points over 10 meetings, while Charlotte versus Portland is the lowest at 197.0 -- a 58-point gap between the league's fastest and slowest recurring games. This describes games already played, not a forecast of any future meeting, and it is not a home/away split.

entries.q: Does slowing the game down really help the underdog?
alt_phrasings: Does pace help the weaker team?
How much does tempo change upset odds?

a.answer: It helps, but only a little. Across the NBA's observed pace range of about 92 to 104 possessions, an 80 percent favorite's upset probability rises only from 19.5 percent at the fastest pace to 20.9 percent at the slowest -- a 1.4-point swing. Fewer possessions mean fewer chances for the better team to separate, but real NBA pace barely moves game to game, so the mechanical effect on any single matchup is small. This isolates the variance mechanism only, holding per-possession scoring fixed.

entries.q: How much does the Pelicans' win probability move with and without Zion?
alt_phrasings: New Orleans with and without Zion

a.answer: In the star-removal exhibit, New Orleans moves from 0.3292 with Zion Williamson to 0.0469 without on a neutral floor versus a league-average team -- a 0.2823 swing, off a low starting team strength. It is a ceiling built from an on/off net-rating delta with a roster confound, descriptive only, not a betting number.

entries.q: What is Wembanyama's star value to San Antonio in this exhibit?

a.answer: San Antonio moves from 0.3901 with Victor Wembanyama to 0.112 without on a neutral floor against a league-average opponent -- a 0.2781 win-prob swing. As with every row, it is a ceiling from a roster-confounded on/off delta, not a controlled individual value, and it is descriptive rather than an edge claim.

entries.q: Does the system know when a late-game lead is basically safe?
alt_phrasings: Is the win-prob model calibrated late in games?
How well does it read game state?

a.answer: In the bulk of regulation states it tracks reality closely: for a 1-to-5 point lead with 24-36 minutes left, the model's mean win probability is 0.6204 across 898 games and teams in that state actually won 62.03 percent of the time. The honest exception is overtime -- with a 1-5 lead in OT the model says 0.7113 while teams actually won 98.3 percent and the market priced 97.6 percent, so it under-rates how decisive a late lead is and the market is better there. This is a calibration exhibit, never a profit claim.

entries.q: Can you give me Jokic's clutch or fourth-quarter splits?
alt_phrasings: How does Jokic play in the clutch?
Fourth quarter per-36 for a player

a.answer: Not from this data. The NBA boxscores table is a full-game aggregate with no period or clutch grain, so a Q4 or overtime per-36 split cannot be computed without fabricating it -- and the module refuses rather than invent one. The per-period box lines do exist in the raw cache, but the ingest step sums them into one full-game row and discards the period grain, so recovering clutch splits is a data-layer re-ingest that is out of scope here.

entries.q: Which teams are best at protecting leads versus storming back?
alt_phrasings: Who holds leads and who rallies?

a.answer: A per-team front-runner-versus-comeback profile is not buildable from this slice: zero of 30 teams clear the floor of at least two games both leading and trailing at halftime in the 26-game corpus, so per-team labels would be 1-2 game noise. The only robust readout is league-level -- second-half margin regresses on halftime margin with a slope of 0.2885, and a team that led at half went on to a +1.346 second-half margin on average. The module declines to print per-team rankings rather than over-claim.

entries.q: Can you give me a player's aging curve or age-adjusted projection?
alt_phrasings: What does the aging curve say?
Is this player past his prime by the model?

a.answer: Aging curves are not buildable from this data. No birthdate or age column exists in any NBA table, and only three season snapshots (2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26) are on hand, while aging-curve methods need age-labeled player-seasons across many seasons. The codebase's own audit reaches the same defer verdict; add age labels and more seasons and it becomes testable.

entries.q: What is this player's RAPM, EPM, or DARKO?
alt_phrasings: Give me an impact metric like EPM
What does DARKO say about him?

a.answer: Those are not reproduced. From 77,744 box-score rows the system can honestly build a box-only value index, per-36 rates, and unadjusted on/off, but RAPM, xRAPM, EPM, DARKO, LEBRON, BPM, and RAPTOR are all marked do-not-fake because the required league-wide RAPM target or continuous tracking inputs do not exist in the repo. Support means raw input-column coverage only, never a claim to reproduce a branded metric under a borrowed name.

entries.q: Can you rank every NBA team by true offensive rating or possessions?
alt_phrasings: Give me real pace and ORtg per team

a.answer: Not at that grain from the team manifest. The team cards carry ppg_latest_season and a pace_proxy, but pace_proxy is explicitly a proxy, not official possession-based pace, and ppg is a single-season average with no schedule or opponent adjustment. A true possession-based offensive rating and official pace are not what this descriptive manifest provides, so ranking teams by them here would overstate what the data supports.

entries.q: Is Jokic's 0.58 win-probability swing a clean measure of his individual value?
alt_phrasings: Can I trust the with/without win prob as player value?
Does star removal isolate one player?

a.answer: No -- it is explicitly a ceiling, not a clean causal player value. The 0.5822 swing comes from attributing a full-lineup on-vs-off net-rating gap to one man, with no control for teammates, opponent, coach trust, or garbage time, and the net-rating-to-Elo conversion is a single frozen constant, not a fit. It is a comparable, honest price tag on star dependence, useful as matchup context but labeled descriptive-only, not an edge or a true individual-value estimate.

entries.q: Does Giannis's high field-goal percentage mean he is a great shooter?
alt_phrasings: Is Giannis a good shooter because of 60 percent FG?
What does Giannis's 60.9 percent really mean?

a.answer: Not in the way it sounds -- his 60.9 percent from the field largely reflects a rim-heavy shot diet, not touch from range. The range and line numbers tell the other half: 27.4 percent from three and 64.0 percent on free throws. So the elite field-goal rate is about where the shots come from, which the raw percentage does not separate from shooting skill.

entries.q: Between Luka and Jokic, who is the steadier producer?
alt_phrasings: Who is more metronomic, Luka or Jokic?
Compare Doncic and Jokic game-to-game variance

a.answer: They are essentially tied at the top, with Luka Doncic just ahead: a shrunk composite coefficient of variation of 0.3448 for Doncic versus 0.3456 for Jokic, both far under the league median of 0.6235 among 579 players. Their nightly production barely wobbles, roughly half the game-to-game variability of a median rotation player. Lower CV means steadier, not necessarily more valuable, and no opponent or rest adjustment is applied.

entries.q: How much does Milwaukee's win probability depend on Giannis in the star-removal exhibit?

a.answer: Milwaukee moves from 0.6059 with Giannis Antetokounmpo to 0.1617 without on a neutral floor versus a league-average team -- a 0.4441 win-prob swing, among the largest for a team's clear lead star. Like every row it is a ceiling from a roster-confounded on/off delta, descriptive and not a causal or betting number.

entries.q: Which is the more reliable star profile, Kawhi Leonard or Kevin Durant on efficiency?
alt_phrasings: Who shoots better across zones, Kawhi or Durant?

a.answer: Both are three-level shooters with nearly matched lines: Kawhi at 51.1 / 40.4 / 87.9 and Durant at 52.3 / 41.8 / 85.8 from the field, three, and the line. Kawhi scores 27.1 points per 36 to Durant's 26.0, and both are low-assist, score-first roles (3.8 and 4.6 assists per 36). These are per-36 rates unadjusted for shot difficulty, so treat them as efficiency profiles, not a ranking of impact.

entries.q: Who is the biggest faller in form over the sample?
alt_phrasings: Which player trended down the most?
Who lost the most box production?

a.answer: Myles Turner is the biggest faller, with his 10-game rolling per-36 box composite down -11.043 over the observed span -- the mirror image of Wembanyama's league-leading +19.821 rise to 37.869. This is a net change over the whole multi-season span, a trajectory read rather than a current streak, and it is box-composite only, not age- or opponent-adjusted.

entries.q: How many players and games sit behind these NBA player numbers?
alt_phrasings: What is the data coverage for player metrics?
How big is the box-score sample?
How many rows feed the player analytics?

a.answer: The box-score layer covers 77,744 player-game rows spanning 807 unique players and 3,611 games, with full box scores at zero percent missing. That coverage supports box-only value, per-36 rates, and unadjusted on/off, but it is the reason branded impact metrics are declined -- the raw inputs for RAPM or continuous tracking are not present. Coverage means input-column completeness, not a claim about any adjusted metric.

entries.q: Is the atlas 'top contributor' the same as a team's best player?
alt_phrasings: Does top contributor mean best player?
What does top contributor actually measure?
Why is a role player listed as top contributor?

a.answer: No -- the 'top contributor' is simply the player with the most total minutes for a team across the sample, not the best or highest-scoring one. That is why Boston's is Derrick White (7,576.2 minutes) and Golden State's is Brandin Podziemski (6,018.4), not the marquee names, while on Denver and Oklahoma City it happens to coincide with the lead star. The metric alongside it, PRA-per-36, is a raw box rate, not an impact measure.

entries.q: How does this system grade itself?
alt_phrasings: how do you check your own work

a.answer: Every named mechanism the system tests is written to an append-only validation ledger with its verdict, effect size, p-value, and the corpus it ran on. The scoreboard over those ledgers currently counts 287 rows across four sports, of which 129 of 256 testable hypotheses survived as confirmed -- a survival rate of 0.5039. A confirmed, a null, and a not-testable are all recorded and counted; a system that only ever confirmed would not be credible.

entries.q: How many of your claims are verified versus null?

a.answer: In the forward claim scoreboard over 259 hypothesis families, 121 are verified, 99 are null, 28 not-testable, 7 retracted, and 4 provisional. That is a ratio of 1.107 nulls-or-worse per confirm. The nulls are kept and published on purpose -- they are the honest shape of a real search, not a defect.

entries.q: Do nulls actually outnumber your confirmed findings?
alt_phrasings: how many things did not work

a.answer: Yes. Across the four sport ledgers plus a 1,003-row interaction-factory sweep, nulls (351) outnumber confirms (168) by about 2.1x. In MLB the balance actually inverts, 32 confirmed against 37 null. Keeping the failures visible is the entire point of the exhibit.

entries.q: What was the biggest result you had to retract?
alt_phrasings: a headline number that fell apart

a.answer: The most-cited retraction was an early pregame return-on-investment headline that turned out to be a market-follow grading artifact: the grader picked bet direction from the market's own devigged favorite and never actually read the model, priced at a flat -110 fiction, with filters tuned in-sample on the same file. Read against real closing lines the model is roughly break-even-minus-vig, about -2.00% unfiltered. The instrument that caught it was built by the same person who made the claim.

entries.q: Tell me about the in-play backtest headline you pulled back.

a.answer: An in-play backtest once posted eye-catching accuracy and return figures on 55,073 bets, but those were settled against a soft L5 rolling-average line proxy, not real sharp closing lines. That makes it a model-quality ceiling, not a tradeable or realized result, so both figures were retracted and no dollar number is quoted in their place. The first real closing-line-value reading is not expected until October 2026.

entries.q: Did you find a leak in your own win-probability model?
alt_phrasings: did a feature peek at the future

a.answer: Yes. The end-of-third-quarter win-probability model was fed two features computed from fourth-quarter data (halftime_pace_shift and trailing_team_q4_usg_hhi), so it was peeking at the quarter it was supposed to predict, and the famous Brier headline was also mis-sourced from the cited file. After removing the two leaking features the honest leak-free walk-forward Brier is about 0.141. It is framed as a leak caught in my own pipeline, not as a competitive number.

entries.q: How big is the reject pile?
alt_phrasings: how many signals did you kill

a.answer: The reject ledger holds 804 recorded verdict rows, of which 628 are on a REJECT-family verdict (627 explicit REJECT) against 95 SHIP and 45 SHIP_REVIEW. As of their latest test, 68 distinct sport-signal pairs currently sit on a reject verdict. A REJECT is honest market-efficiency evidence, not a failure -- no dollar or edge claim rides on any of it.

entries.q: Why do you reject so many signals?
alt_phrasings: most common reason for a reject
why does the gate kill candidates

a.answer: By reason category, the largest bucket of rejects is the as-of reclaim sweep at 510, followed by prescreen-delta (20), walk-forward ablation (18), and seed-stability (17). By sport the reject rows split NBA 426, soccer 205, MLB 118, tennis 55. Most candidates simply do not clear a leak-free gate that was built to refute, not confirm.

entries.q: Does the system claim a betting edge?

a.answer: No. Every committed analytics artifact carries edge_claimed=false, and against real closing lines the finding is that the market is efficient. This is a calibrated predictor whose honest win is matching the devigged close within noise, plus a measured in-game conditioning improvement -- not a dollar edge. Accuracy is not edge, and an honest reject is treated as a success.

entries.q: How well does the model do against the market's own probabilities?
alt_phrasings: do you beat the market's Brier
is the model sharper than the price

a.answer: It does not beat the market's Brier. The in-game Brier skill score of model versus market is at or below zero everywhere: for MLB all-innings the model Brier is 0.237684 against the market's 0.206653 (skill score -0.1502), and for international soccer all-minutes it is 0.227887 against 0.142726 (skill score -0.5967). Both model and market crush the base-rate baseline, which is expected and is not an edge.

entries.q: What did the full-season backtest actually prove?
alt_phrasings: are you well calibrated but not profitable

a.answer: The full-season leak-free walk-forward backtest (with truncation-invariance proven) shows the model is well-calibrated but does not beat the close: season Brier 0.208 versus the closing line's 0.198. Spread and total pregame closing-line value is essentially zero, with correlation-with-outcome of 0.001. That negative result is exactly what a rigorous validation framework is supposed to produce.

entries.q: What is the one measured win the system does claim?

a.answer: The one measured calibration win is in-game conditioning: fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state sharpens the win-probability forecaster, moving Brier from 0.209 to 0.159 for NBA and 0.241 to 0.126 for MLB on real out-of-sample corpora. It is labeled calibration, not a dollar edge, because a live book sees the score too. edge_claimed stays false.

entries.q: What happened in the playoff replay validation?
alt_phrasings: did you have a playoff edge

a.answer: Replaying the Finals games G1 through G3 through the in-game projector produced a pooled win-probability Brier of 0.34 to 0.40 in-series -- worse than a coin flip. That is the cleanest proof in the system that the playoff market is efficient and there is no pregame playoff edge. It is reported as an honest negative result.

entries.q: How was this AI actually built?

a.answer: It is a solo human-architected build over an agentic pipeline: across 3,224 commits from 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-22, about 95.75% are agent-authored and 67.9% carry a Claude co-author trailer. The busiest single day logged 275 commits. The honest framing is one human directing the pipeline and owning the ship/reject and validation decisions, not one person hand-typing thousands of commits.

entries.q: Was this really built over 13 months?
alt_phrasings: how long did the build take

a.answer: No -- an earlier 13-month figure is not supported by git and was dropped. The commit history spans 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-22, roughly four and a half months. The honest description is an intensive solo build across that window.

entries.q: How many fact-claims has the system generated, and how many are actually verified?

a.answer: The claims corpus holds 103,048 generated fact-claims across 103 families; 99 families carry a validation sidecar and 4 do not. Of 101,865 claims sampled for validation, 101,864 verified with 0 mismatches and 1 unverifiable -- covering 98.85% of generated claims. The metadata is explicit that generated outnumbers verified by design, so 'verified' never silently means 'generated'.

entries.q: Did you once claim more verified claims than you could back up?
alt_phrasings: a claim count with no artifact

a.answer: Yes -- an earlier figure of roughly 52,343 verified claims has no surviving artifact and is not claimed. The corpus is now presented as its honest split instead: 103,048 generated fact-claims with a validation sample verifying 101,864 of 101,865 sampled. The generated/validated distinction is stated up front on purpose.

entries.q: Which sports have the most tested hypotheses, and how many held up?

a.answer: By survival rate, NBA leads at 0.56 (42 confirmed of 75 testable), tennis 0.5455, soccer 0.5179, and MLB the lowest at 0.3974. Across all four the overall survival rate is 0.5039 on 256 testable hypotheses. Roughly half surviving is the expected shape when the gate is genuinely trying to refute each candidate.

entries.q: What kinds of effects survive your gate, and which mostly fail?
alt_phrasings: do rest and fatigue signals hold up

a.answer: By category, officiating effects survive best at 0.75 and the small travel bucket at 1.0, while rest-and-fatigue effects survive weakest at just 0.3056 (11 of 36 testable). That is a useful honesty signal: the folk-wisdom rest-and-fatigue story mostly does not replicate under a leak-free gate. Every bucket is reported as-is, with no dollar or edge claim attached.

entries.q: Give me an example of a mechanism that did confirm.

a.answer: The back-to-back rest penalty in NBA confirmed with an effect of -1.73 points of margin (p=0.005645) on a 4,732-row corpus, meaning teams on zero days rest averaged worse margins than those with a day off. Home-court advantage also confirmed at about 3.4 points. The ledger stores each with its p-value and corpus so the number can be reproduced, not taken on faith.

entries.q: Give me an example of a mechanism that came back null.

a.answer: Rest-differential-versus-margin came back null: the correlation between home-minus-away rest and home margin was about -0.018 with p well above any threshold, so no usable effect. A star-injury usage-vacuum event study and pace-mismatch variance also landed null. These sit in the same ledger as the confirms, counted rather than quietly dropped.

entries.q: Do any of your findings flip verdict when you re-test them?

a.answer: Yes, and the system keeps the whole history rather than the flattering last row. Five families are flagged as flipped -- for example NBA three-in-four fatigue went null then confirmed on a larger corpus, and an MLB staff-day-after fatigue chain went null, confirmed, then null again. A positive full-sample lift that sign-flips out of sample is treated as the overfit signature and caught, not published.

entries.q: How many hypotheses has the interaction factory tested?

a.answer: The interaction factory that composes confirmed single-mechanism findings into two-way candidates has adjudicated 1,003 of them: 709 not-testable, 239 null, 38 confirmed, and 17 failed-replication. The large not-testable and null majority is the gate doing its job, not a shortfall. The not-testable rows are untested combinations, evidence for nothing either way.

entries.q: Does the answer engine ever refuse to answer?
alt_phrasings: can the system say no data

a.answer: Yes, refusing is a designed behavior. In a 1,307-question coverage stress test the status split was 399 ok, 560 no_data, 42 not_supported, 181 ambiguous, 125 refused, and 0 errors, for an honest coverage rate of 0.3662 on the questions that expect an answer. A correct no_data or not_supported is scored as a design pass, not a failure -- the engine is fail-closed rather than improvising.

entries.q: What happens when someone asks the system for an edge or ROI?
alt_phrasings: how does it handle profit questions

a.answer: It refuses all of them. In the coverage stress test the edge-language category had 125 questions with an ok-rate of 0.0 -- every single one was refused -- and the prediction-winprob category likewise refused all 85. That refusal is enforced by the no-edge rail, not left to a model's discretion.

entries.q: Is the answer-engine regression bank passing?

a.answer: Yes -- the answer-quality regression bank runs 87 checks and all 87 pass at the FULL tier, with 0 failures. Those are fail-closed status and receipt checks: a correct no_data, not_supported, or ambiguous response counts as a pass. It measures answer consistency, not any edge.

entries.q: Do the public showcase numbers actually reproduce?
alt_phrasings: can I reproduce the site numbers

a.answer: Every showcase builder module carries a self-check, and the latest check-all report shows all of them returning PASS. Separately, the repo's check_all self-check passes 52 of 52 on a bare clone and runs green in public CI, where the trail also preserves the first run that honestly failed 46 of 52 on a path-portability bug before it was fixed. Keeping the red run in the history is the discipline, not an embarrassment.

entries.q: What is the model's prop-stat accuracy, and is it leak-free?
alt_phrasings: how accurate are the player projections

a.answer: On a 20,354-row production-model chronological holdout (last 20% by date, run through the production inference path), the mean absolute errors are PTS 4.83, REB 1.92, AST 1.39, and FG3M 0.89. The verify script fail-closes if any stat drifts more than 0.02 from these. It is leak-free and competitive with published prop-model benchmarks, and this holdout set is the honest lead accuracy claim.

entries.q: What is the win-probability model's headline accuracy?
alt_phrasings: how good is the win probability

a.answer: The five-way NNLS win-probability stack reads 0.709 accuracy and 0.193 Brier under three-fold walk-forward validation. That is a calibration number, reported without any claim that it beats a closing line -- the full-season test shows it does not.

entries.q: Do the computer-vision features add predictive value today?
alt_phrasings: do tracking features help the model

a.answer: Not yet. Every CV-derived feature carries SHAP importance of about 0.0 in the production prop models today, and the CV-lift report reads has_cv_data false. The plumbing is complete and the thesis is credible, but it is honestly labeled as not-yet-a-measured-edge rather than a moat.

entries.q: How many games has the tracking pipeline actually processed?

a.answer: The CV features table holds 17,254 rows across 241 games covering 252 distinct real NBA player IDs, with 29 distinct feature names. The volume is real, but the file itself notes these are coverage stats only -- no accuracy or MOT metric is claimed, because those are not benchmarked against labeled ground truth.

entries.q: How many players does the tracker actually hold per game?

a.answer: Across the tracked games the distinct-players-per-game averages 2.63 with a maximum of 8, so the claim of reliable 10-player broadcast tracking is not demonstrated. The detector finds all ten players, but stable slot identity across occlusions is limited. Those are volume figures with no positional-accuracy claim attached.

entries.q: How complete are the per-player dossiers?
alt_phrasings: how full are the player profiles

a.answer: There are 1,249 dossiers spanning 28 categories, with a median completeness score of 0.464. Fill rates vary widely and honestly: rebounding profile is well-filled at 0.9544 and foul-drawing at 0.8655, while pace-fit (0.0104), turnover profile (0.0144), and matchup splits (0.0849) are sparse. The gaps are surfaced rather than hidden.

entries.q: Is the re-identification network trained on NBA footage?
alt_phrasings: did you train the re-ID model

a.answer: No. The shipped OSNet weights are ImageNet-pretrained, not NBA-fine-tuned, and the production appearance model is actually the HSV color histogram. The honest claim is that the OSNet omni-scale architecture was reimplemented in PyTorch and runs with ImageNet weights -- not that a deep re-ID model was trained on basketball.

entries.q: How accurate is per-player CV attribution?
alt_phrasings: can you attribute tracking to individuals

a.answer: Per-player CV attribution is about 4% accurate -- slot identities are not stable across long occlusions. Aggregate team-level and position-level CV features are ship-ready, but individual attribution is openly documented as weak. This is stated in the known-limitations file rather than buried.

entries.q: Are all your tests passing?

a.answer: Not 100%. There are roughly 7,400 tests collected, passing at about 97 to 98% locally, with a documented tail from DB, GPU, optional-dependency, and version drift plus a native pyarrow segfault on Windows. The critical betting-math core and in-play subsets pass clean, and a full-green claim is explicitly not made.

entries.q: Is there a known bug you have not fixed yet?

a.answer: Yes -- the sim_win_prob feature is polarity-inverted at the source, with correlation to home-won of about -0.194, and it remains unpatched because the fix needs a coordinated model retrain cascade. The v1 models learned to flip it internally so they are fine, but the in-play heads carry a silent effect. It is surfaced publicly precisely because it is real, measurable, and not yet fixed.

entries.q: How big and how separated is the codebase?

a.answer: The codebase is about 430 Python modules, and roughly 130 of them under the prediction folder are a research surface with only about 12 load-bearing in the live deployment graph. The FastAPI layer serves about 99 endpoints across 12 routers. Being explicit that most of the surface is experiment, not production, is a judgment claim, not a size brag.

entries.q: How many mechanism hypotheses have you closed across all sports?

a.answer: The knowledge-engine mechanism ledger currently exports 287 rows across four sports, bucketed as 130 confirmed, 126 null, and 31 not-testable. A large null share is the expected shape of a real audit, and every row keeps its verdict, effect size, p-value, and source corpus. No dollar or edge claim rides on any of them.

entries.q: Does the paper-trading ledger prove you make money?
alt_phrasings: does the paper ledger show profit

a.answer: No. The paper execution ledger has 83 logged bets, every one with executed=false -- none were real fills -- and realized closing-line-value is null for all 37 settled rows because no independent close feed was captured for that channel. The only quantity it can speak to is placement-time divergence (model versus taken price), median about 0.092 probability points, which is an execution measurement, not a proven edge. It records no-close honestly rather than backfilling a number.

entries.q: Has any real money been placed?

a.answer: Zero real money has been placed, by design. It is gated behind a sharp-book closing-line-value reading that cannot start until October 2026, plus CV-depth and deployment-stability work. Until that gate runs, no real-money execution is considered justified.

entries.q: Across sports, does the model beat the market at any game state?
alt_phrasings: any state where model is sharper
where does model win vs market

a.answer: Mostly no. Across 17 cross-sport rows, most are underpowered (confidence interval spans zero) or market-sharper -- for example NBA end-of-first-quarter win-probability has a paired delta of -0.0084, flagged market-sharper and still provisional. The only model-sharper rows are late-inning MLB total-runs, and even those are labeled provisional pending more data. Every row is reported as-is.

entries.q: Where does the model lose to the market -- calibration or information?

a.answer: It is mostly an information gap, not a calibration one. The Murphy decomposition shows the MLB model Brier of 0.2377 trails the market's 0.2067 (a gap of +0.0310) driven mainly by resolution, and the soccer model's 0.2279 trails 0.1427 the same way. Resolution gaps are information the market has and the model does not -- they cannot be closed by recalibration.

entries.q: How many claims per sport does the corpus hold?

a.answer: By sport the generated claims break down as NBA 62,227, MLB 21,519, tennis 13,709, and soccer 4,275, with smaller unlabeled cross-sport and WNBA sets. All are ranking-kind claims validated against their own sidecars, with edge_claimed false throughout. The counts are volume of descriptive statements, not proven edges.

entries.q: Is the aggregate closing-line-value figure you once cited real?

a.answer: No -- an earlier aggregate closing-line-value figure was circular, computed on the same corpus where the model was never actually read. No real Pinnacle-close CLV exists yet; the full-season backtest shows CLV near zero versus real closes. So no CLV number is quoted; only the methodology that will eventually measure it is built.

entries.q: Was the assists edge you talked up ever real?

a.answer: It was retracted on 2026-07-21 as regime-dependent -- it broke in the playoffs, and the in-series PBP replay confirmed no model edge in playoff games. Under the no-edge rail, no dollar or ROI edge is claimed anywhere; the assist candidate stands as an honest reject, not a live edge. The historical measurement stays in the gate artifacts only as a record of the stress-testing method.

entries.q: What is the honest read on the overall betting result versus real closes?

a.answer: Against real DraftKings, FanDuel, and MGM closing lines the model is roughly break-even-minus-vig overall, about -2% to -5%, with -2.00% unfiltered from the gate analysis. The market is efficient on closing lines. Every candidate edge, including the strongest one, was ultimately rejected or retracted by my own gates.

entries.q: How much of the in-game MAE improvement is real skill versus just mechanical?
alt_phrasings: how much of the 46% is skill

a.answer: Most of it is mechanical. The end-of-Q3 residual heads cut prediction MAE by about 46% pooled, but three of four quarters of box score are simply observed by then; over a naive carry-forward in-game baseline the learned-head value-add is about 26%, walk-forward validated. The honest framing states it that way rather than claiming the full 46% as skill, and the MAE lift is never bundled with the leaked endQ3 Brier.

entries.q: How was the answer engine designed to stay honest about what it does not know?
alt_phrasings: how does it avoid making things up

a.answer: It routes every question through a resolver registry that maps each supported question type to exactly one deterministic source and refuses anything unregistered rather than improvising. In the coverage stress test that produced 560 no_data and 125 refused out of 1,307 questions, all treated as design passes. Every mechanism answer carries its verdict, sample size, p-value, and source file, so it is reproduced byte-for-byte rather than free-associated.

entries.q: Do you keep retracted findings in the ledger or delete them?

a.answer: They are kept and counted. The forward claim scoreboard explicitly holds 7 retracted families alongside 121 verified and 99 null, and the story field states that a system which only ever confirmed would not be credible. Verdict history is ordered by run timestamp so a flip is visible, not overwritten.

entries.q: Which categories does the answer engine answer well versus refuse?

a.answer: Deterministic, source-backed categories answer well: win-probability at ok-rate 1.0, calibration numbers 0.963, matchup previews 0.8889, and verified claims 0.6512. Categories that would require an edge or an unbacked opinion refuse hardest: edge-language, prediction-winprob, and mechanism-effect all sit at 0.0. The split is the design working as intended.

entries.q: What share of commits did a human hand-author?

a.answer: About 95.75% of the 3,224 commits are agent-authored, so roughly 4% were hand-authored by the human. Around 67.9% carry a Claude co-author trailer. The honest description is a human architect and director of an agentic build pipeline who owns the engineering judgment and the ship-or-reject decisions.

entries.q: What is the system's realized ROI?

a.answer: There is no realized ROI to report: zero real money has been placed, and no dollar or ROI edge is claimed anywhere, with edge_claimed=false on every artifact. The paper execution ledger's 83 logged bets are all executed=false, and realized closing-line-value is null for the settled rows. The honest yardstick, better-than-close CLV, cannot be measured until an independent close feed accumulates from October 2026.

entries.q: What is your Sharpe ratio or bankroll growth?

a.answer: No Sharpe ratio or bankroll-growth figure exists, because no real money has been staked and the paper ledger is units-only with no dollars. Any such number would require realized returns the system does not have. The system reports this gap rather than manufacturing a figure.

entries.q: Can you tell me the system's percentage edge over the sportsbook?

a.answer: No edge figure is provided -- this is a calibrated predictor, not an edge product, and the no-edge rail refuses edge and ROI language outright. In the answer-engine stress test all 125 edge-language questions were refused, ok-rate 0.0. Against real closes the honest finding is that the market is efficient.

entries.q: What is your current closing-line-value track record?

a.answer: There is no realized closing-line-value track record yet: in the paper execution ledger, clv_pct is null for all 37 settled rows because no independent close feed was captured for that channel. No historical sharp-book closing archive exists publicly either, so the first real reading is roughly October 2026 onward. The methodology to measure it is built; the number is honestly absent.

entries.q: Does the possession simulator have a proven betting edge?

a.answer: No betting edge is claimed for the possession simulator -- only its structure is validated. The correct negative teammate correlation of about -0.10 emerges from the mechanics with no hand-tuned matrix, and the same-game-parlay pricing is structurally correct, but there is no real parlay-price capture to grade against. Team totals also run slightly high, so the side is trusted more than the over.

entries.q: Does the system have a real-money profit track record I can look at?

a.answer: There is no real-money profit track record, by design -- zero money has been placed and the paper ledger's bets are all executed=false. Today's snapshot returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA for CLV, because no close was captured. What exists is a units-only paper track and the harnesses that will grade a real one once a sharp-book close feed accumulates.

entries.q: Is the Kelly bankroll sizing fully calibrated?

a.answer: Not fully -- the Kelly correlation matrix is currently unpopulated, so until it is computed the sizing assumes independent bets, which overstates max-loss risk on correlated slates. The fractional-Kelly machinery (quarter-Kelly, drawdown breaker, isotonic-calibrated input) exists, but this specific calibration input is a known gap. It is disclosed rather than assumed complete.

entries.q: What is the honest one-line summary of what this system is?

a.answer: It is a calibrated multi-sport forecasting system whose strongest signal is that the same builder built the instruments that caught and retracted his own inflated headline numbers. The market-efficiency finding -- well-calibrated but does not beat the close -- is the cleanest output a rigorous validation framework can produce. Accuracy is not edge, and honest rejects are counted as successes.
